title: Coordinating the Community Garden
description: Edit a full informational passage for grammar, punctuation, usage, and clarity.
subject: rla
passage:
The Oak Street Community Garden is preparing for its busiest planting weekend of the year. More than sixty volunteers have registered for Saturday, and several local organizations are donating tools, soil, and seedlings. The volunteer coordinator is revising a message that explains arrival times, work groups, and what participants should bring.

Volunteers will check in at the north gate between 8:30 and 9:00 a.m. After checking in, each person will receive a colored card showing a work area. Green cards are for the vegetable beds, blue cards are for the rain garden, and yellow cards are for the tool-cleaning station. The coordinator asks volunteers to bring a refillable water bottle, closed shoes, and sun protection.

The garden has enough hand tools for most tasks, but volunteers who own work gloves are encouraged to bring them. A small number of wheelbarrows will be shared among the groups. Because the site has narrow paths, the coordinator does not want volunteers to leave bags or personal items beside the beds. A storage tent near the entrance will be available throughout the morning.

The message also explains what happens if heavy rain begins before the event. Organizers will post a decision on the garden website by 7:00 a.m. Saturday. If the event is delayed, registered volunteers will also receive an email. The coordinator wants the final message to be friendly, but it must still use standard English and make every instruction easy to follow on a phone screen.

The coordinator is also checking the message against the signs that will be posted at the entrance. The email does not need to repeat every word on those signs, but the names of work areas and check-in locations must match. A volunteer who reads “north gate” in the email should not arrive and find a sign that calls the same place the “main entrance.” Consistent wording matters because many participants will be visiting the garden for the first time.

A final review will focus on instructions that contain words such as only, before, and after. The coordinator wants those limiting words placed next to the idea they actually modify. She is also shortening sentences that contain several separate commands. The purpose is not to make the message casual; it is to make each action clear enough that volunteers can follow it without stopping to interpret the grammar.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: “Each of the volunteers {{blank}} a colored work card.”
questions.explanation: The subject 'each' is singular and takes 'receives'.
questions.rule: Do not let a plural noun inside an of-phrase control the verb.

options.text: receive
options.whyWrong: 'Each' is singular even though 'volunteers' is plural.

options.text: have received
options.whyWrong: This plural verb phrase does not agree with 'each'.

options.text: were receiving
receives

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest pronoun revision: “When volunteers put bags beside the beds, they can block the paths.”
questions.explanation: The revision names 'bags' as the things that can block the paths.
questions.rule: Replace a pronoun when two possible antecedents could change the meaning.

options.text: When volunteers put bags beside the beds, they can block the paths.
options.whyWrong: 'They' could refer to the volunteers or the bags.

options.text: Bags left beside the beds can block the paths.
When they put them beside them, they can block the paths.
options.whyWrong: The repeated pronouns make the sentence much less clear.

options.text: The paths can block them when volunteers put bags beside the beds.

questions.explanation: The conditional clause is attached to a complete main clause.
questions.rule: An if-clause needs a main clause to complete the thought.

options.text: If heavy rain begins before the event.
options.whyWrong: This dependent clause is a fragment.

options.text: If heavy rain begins before the event, and.
If heavy rain begins before the event, organizers will post an update.
Because heavy rain begins. Organizers will post an update.
options.whyWrong: The first sentence is a dependent-clause fragment.

questions.prompt: Choose the most concise revision: “Volunteers who have their own personal work gloves may bring them.”
questions.explanation: The sentence keeps the permission and item while removing redundant wording.
questions.rule: Remove repeated ownership words and unnecessary phrases.

options.text: Volunteers with work gloves may bring them.
Volunteers who have their own personal work gloves may bring them.
options.whyWrong: 'Own personal' is redundant, and 'who have' can be shortened here.

options.text: Volunteers personally owning their own gloves may bring those gloves themselves.
options.whyWrong: This adds repeated ownership and unnecessary words.

options.text: In the event that volunteers possess gloves personally, they may bring them.
options.whyWrong: This is inflated and less direct.

questions.prompt: The paths are narrow; {{blank}}, bags should be stored in the entrance tent.
questions.explanation: 'Therefore' shows that the storage rule follows from the narrow-path condition.
questions.rule: Choose the transition after naming the relationship in plain words.

options.text: however
options.whyWrong: The storage instruction is a result of the narrow paths, not a contrast.

options.text: for example
options.whyWrong: The storage rule is not an example of narrow paths.

options.text: meanwhile
options.whyWrong: The relationship is cause/result, not simultaneous timing.

options.text: therefore

questions.prompt: Choose the correct possessive: “The {{blank}} website will post the rain decision.”
questions.explanation: One garden owns or operates the website, so garden's is correct.
questions.rule: For one owner, use singular noun + apostrophe + s.

options.text: gardens
options.whyWrong: This plural form does not show possession.

options.text: garden's
gardens'
options.whyWrong: This would mean the website belongs to multiple gardens.

options.text: garden's'
options.whyWrong: A singular possessive takes only apostrophe + s.
